title: Camus
summary: Camus started from “the absurd” — the collision between the human hunger for meaning and clarity and a silent, indifferent world. His answer is not despair but revolt: to live fully and lucidly, without pretending that a final answer has been found, and to choose life, solidarity and love of the world again and again. “One must imagine Sisyphus happy.”
onEmotions: Camus did not build a theory of emotions, but his philosophy is very much about feelings: wonder, weariness, the longing for unity, the love of life. He believed that awareness of the absurd often begins not with a thought but with a feeling — a sudden “why?”, a weariness with mechanical routine. He valued “lucidity” (lucidité) — the ability to see your feelings honestly, without comforting illusions but also without despair. And he insisted on a passion for life: the sun, the sea, the body, friendship and solidarity were not trifles for Camus but the very heart of what makes life worth living.

anxiety.text: “This world in itself is not reasonable, that is all that can be said,” Camus wrote — and the line is oddly calming. Anxiety is a natural response to a world that gives no guarantees. Camus called “the absurd” the collision between the human hunger for clarity and the silence of the world: we want to know that everything will be all right, and the world does not answer. He proposed “lucidity” (lucidité): seeing uncertainty honestly and still living fully, here and now. Anxiety is not an error of the mind but the voice of your hunger for meaning, and it tells you how much life matters to you. There is no need to suppress it; you can admit that there are no guarantees — and return to what is here right now: your breath, the light, your work, people.
anxiety.practice: Step into the light — at a window or outside — and feel it on your face for a minute. Tell yourself: “No guarantees, but there is the sun.”

fear.text: In occupied Paris Camus edited the underground paper Combat and ran risks every day — he knew fear from experience, not from books. In The Plague the city is sealed off, the epidemic is unpredictable, and fear becomes part of everyday life. But the novel’s hero, Dr. Rieux, does not pretend to be fearless: he simply keeps doing his job. He says it is not a matter of heroism but of decency — of each person doing their work. Camus shows that courage is not the absence of fear but the ability to act alongside it, and not alone but together with others. So there is no need to be ashamed of fear. You can acknowledge it and ask yourself what “work of your own,” however small, is within your reach right now.
fear.practice: Do one small piece of “your own work” today — not instead of the fear but together with it, like Dr. Rieux, who simply kept working.

sadness.text: Camus is called the philosopher of sun and sea, but he knew that light and shadow cannot be separated, and he did not treat sadness as an enemy. If you are sad right now, it belongs to the same life he loved so much. A lucid view of life, for Camus, includes its sorrow too: there is no need to turn away either from the beauty of the world or from its pain. In his early collection of essays, Betwixt and Between, he wrote that there is no love of life without despair about life — meaning that the intensity of feeling alive and its sadness grow from the same root. That means sadness is not a defeat but part of lucidity: you are seeing life as it is, in all its fragility. And that is exactly why you can love it even more. Sadness does not cancel the joy of living — it deepens it.
sadness.practice: Spend a minute looking at the shadow of any object in the light. Then ask: “What love of life does this sadness reveal in me?”

quote.text: There is no sun without shadow, and it is essential to know the night.
quote.author: Albert Camus

grief.text: A forty-year-old man stands in Saint-Brieuc at the grave of the father he never knew and suddenly realizes that his father was younger than he is — and he is flooded with tenderness. This scene from Camus’s The First Man doesn’t explain or justify grief, neither his nor yours. For him, death is part of the absurd: it has no “reasonable” explanation that would make a loss fair. But his answer is not resignation to meaninglessness; it is revolt: the inner “no, it should not be like this” is a legitimate response in which love of life can be heard. In The Plague, Dr. Rieux loses his wife and his friend, and still stays with people, to bear witness and to remember. Then grief is a form of faithfulness: by remembering and loving, we keep the bond alive.
grief.practice: If you wish, call up one vivid, concrete memory of the one you have lost, and stay with it in silence, as with a warm light.

loneliness.text: Meursault sits on his balcony and spends a whole Sunday watching the street — this is solitude in The Stranger, without complaint and without words. If you feel alone, Camus understood this well. Meursault lives as if apart from shared rituals and expectations, and society never forgives him for being different. But Camus did not stop at estrangement. In The Rebel he arrived at an important idea: each of us experiences the absurd alone, but revolt against injustice and meaninglessness is what unites people. When one person says “no” to suffering, they say it for others too. In other words, your loneliness is not proof that you are a stranger but an experience known to a great many people, and through it you can recognize “your own.” Loneliness then becomes not a wall but a bridge to people who feel something similar.
loneliness.practice: Think of someone — a living person or the author of a book — who felt what you feel, and say one sentence to them out loud, as to a comrade.

anger.text: A slave who has taken orders all his life suddenly turns and says “no” — this is how The Rebel begins. Camus would understand the fury rising in you. For Camus, the central concept is “revolt” (révolte). A rebel, he wrote, is someone who says “no,” but in refusing he does not renounce: his “no” also contains a “yes” — the affirmation of a limit and of values that must not be violated. A slave who refuses to obey affirms that there is something in him that deserves respect. In this light, your anger may be pointing to such a value. But Camus also warned of something else: a revolt that loses its sense of “measure” and starts to justify any cruelty betrays itself. Genuine revolt keeps its respect for the human being — including the opponent. You can accept anger as an honest “no” and ask what “yes” stands behind it.
anger.practice: Stand up straight, plant your feet firmly and say under your breath: “No — to …” and “Yes — to …”. Feel where in your body each word lives.

shame.text: Meursault didn’t cry at his mother’s funeral — and the court in The Stranger judges him for that almost more harshly than for the act itself. Shame is heavy and almost always tied to other people’s expectations; Camus showed this with merciless clarity. Camus himself later explained that his hero is condemned because he “doesn’t play the game.” Camus would probably say that many of our shames are a fear of not matching the ritual, someone else’s script of the “right” feelings. Lucidity (lucidité) helps separate the two: where I really violated something important, and where I simply didn’t match an expectation. Your feelings do not have to look “the way they’re supposed to.”
shame.practice: Imagine yourself in Meursault’s place before the court and ask: “Did I do something bad — or did I simply not play someone else’s game?”

guilt.text: The former lawyer Clamence sits in the Mexico City bar in Amsterdam, confessing to a chance companion — this is how The Fall (1956) begins. Guilt is heavy, and Camus thought about it deeply. Clamence discovers guilt in himself and turns it into endless self-accusation, which at the same time becomes a way of judging everyone around him. Camus shows that this kind of guilt is a closed circle that fixes nothing and makes no one better. The Plague shows another path. Tarrou says that each of us is in one way or another implicated in the evil of the world — and that is why it is worth trying at least not to add to it, and to stand on the side of those who suffer. So guilt can be turned not into self-punishment but into care: what can I do right now to make things a little better?
guilt.practice: Replace the question “How guilty am I?” with Tarrou’s question: “What is one thing I can do right now to make things a little better?” — and do it.

envy.text: Sisyphus does not envy the gods — he has his own rock, and Camus asks us to imagine him happy. Envy is unpleasant, but very human. Camus hardly wrote about it directly, but if we extend his thought, envy often feeds on the hope that somewhere, for someone, life is “solved” — full of meaning, well arranged, clear — while mine is not. Camus, however, saw the absurd as the common condition of all people: no one has received a final answer from the world, even if it looks that way from outside. Envy can soften when you remember that you see only the surface of another person’s life, and that your own “rock” is yours alone. And in the way you carry it there is a truth of your own that no one can take from you.
envy.practice: Imagine that the person you envy also has a rock you cannot see. What might it be?

emptiness.text: In Prague, alone and nearly penniless, the twenty-two-year-old Camus suddenly felt that everything around him had lost its meaning — and then in Italy the light, the hills and simple life gave him back his sense of the world. He knew that hollowness from the inside — and knew it was not the last word. For Camus, such moments are an awakening of consciousness, not a verdict. In The Myth of Sisyphus he came to the idea that life does not need a meaning given in advance to be worth living — on the contrary, it can be lived all the more fully without one. Then emptiness is the moment when the familiar stage sets have fallen, and behind them life itself gradually shows through: light, the body, people.
emptiness.practice: Choose one simple sensation available right now — light, a taste, a sound — and live it fully for a minute, without asking “what for?”

confusion.text: “I don’t know whether this world has a meaning that transcends it,” Camus admitted in The Myth of Sisyphus — and he was not ashamed of not knowing. Confusion, when the world doesn’t explain itself, is a natural response. Camus believed this is not a personal malfunction but the basic human situation: we long for unity, clarity, an understandable meaning, and the world answers with silence. That is the absurd. Camus suggested not looking for a hasty way out — neither in despair nor in a ready-made system that explains everything — but learning to live inside this tension while keeping your “lucidity.” In other words, confusion is an honest admission that you don’t know everything, and such an admission takes courage. It is no reason to stop: you can act without final answers, relying on the little that is already clear now.
confusion.practice: Divide a page into two parts: “What I don’t know” and “What is still clear to me.” Even one line in the second column is already something to stand on.

quote.text: The absurd is born of this confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world.
quote.author: Albert Camus

fatigue.text: “One must imagine Sisyphus happy” — the last line of The Myth of Sisyphus is written about a man who is very tired. Tiredness is real, and Camus understood it like no one else. His central image is Sisyphus, who rolls his rock up the mountain again and again, and again and again it rolls back down. But what interests Camus most is not the climb but the moment when Sisyphus walks back down to the foot of the mountain: this is the “hour of consciousness,” a pause in which he sees his situation clearly. Camus does not demand heroism or urge you to “push harder.” We must imagine Sisyphus happy not because the rock is light but because Sisyphus himself owns his attitude toward it. In this light, the pause, the descent, the breather are a legitimate and important part of the way.
fatigue.practice: Find your own “walk down the mountain” today — a minute between tasks — and live it doing nothing, simply looking around.

boredom.text: “Rising, streetcar, four hours in the office, lunch, streetcar, four hours of work, dinner, sleep” — day after day, until one day the stage sets collapse: this list from The Myth of Sisyphus is familiar to anyone who is bored. Camus saw in boredom the beginning of philosophy. And suddenly the question “why?” arises. For Camus, that is where everything begins: weariness with a mechanical life awakens consciousness. After that, a person either returns to the old rut or wakes up for good. Camus proposed the second path — not necessarily changing your life abruptly, but starting to see it clearly, noticing what automatism had hidden. Boredom is not empty time but a chance to wake up.
boredom.practice: Take one habitual action — your commute, washing the dishes — and do it today as if for the first time.

joy.text: “In the spring, Tipasa is inhabited by gods” — so begin the essays of Nuptials, Camus’s sunniest pages. Joy is at the very center of his philosophy, although he is often thought of as gloomy. He writes about sun, sea, the smell of wormwood, about the happiness of a body that simply lives. For Camus, a lucid understanding of the absurd does not cancel happiness — on the contrary, the two are inseparable: happiness does not need guarantees of eternity to be real. Joy for him is not naivety or an escape from the truth but faithfulness to life itself. So rejoicing while knowing the difficulties of the world is also a form of revolt. Joy does not need to be postponed, hidden in shame or justified: it is a legitimate response to the fact that we are alive and the world around us is beautiful.
joy.practice: Find one thing that delights your body right now — warmth, light, a taste, movement — and stay with it for a minute, doing nothing else.

quote.text: Happiness and the absurd are two sons of the same earth. They are inseparable.
quote.author: Albert Camus

love.text: One night in the midst of the epidemic, Dr. Rieux and Tarrou swim in the warm sea, and for an hour they have nothing but friendship and peace — one of the brightest episodes in The Plague. For Camus, love and tenderness are among the highest values, alongside friendship and solidarity. His philosophy of the absurd is not cold at all: it is full of love for the world, for people, for the body, for the sea. For Camus, love does not need eternity to be real: it is precious here and now, in concrete gestures and encounters. That means tenderness is one of the clearest forms of faithfulness to life. You can accept it wholly, without demanding guarantees from it and without fearing its fragility.
love.practice: Tell someone close about one concrete moment when it was good to be with them — for no reason and without conclusions.

gratitude.text: “Dear Monsieur Germain…” — a few days after the Nobel Prize, Camus wrote to his old schoolteacher. Gratitude, for him, is above all gratitude to the world: to the sun, the sea, the body, people. He grew up poor in Algeria and later wrote that poverty was never a misfortune for him, because the sun shone on it. In the letter he admitted that without the hand he held out to a poor child, none of this would have happened. Then gratitude does not contradict lucidity: the world does not promise meaning, but it gives light, people, moments. Gratitude is a form of love for life as it is, without demands and without conditions.
gratitude.practice: Write a short letter in Camus’s manner — “Dear…” — to someone who once held out a hand to you. You don’t have to send it.

hope.text: “In the midst of winter, I found there was, within me, an invincible summer,” Camus wrote. His relationship with hope is complicated, and it is worth understanding it rightly. In The Myth of Sisyphus he was suspicious of the kind of hope that draws us away from the present — toward “later,” toward a meaning that will come from somewhere outside and justify everything. He believed such hope can rob us of today. But this is not a sermon of hopelessness. Camus believed in human beings and in solidarity, in the idea that revolt against evil makes sense. The Plague ends with Rieux’s thought that there are more things to admire in people than to despise. In other words, hope is not waiting for rescue but an inner strength that lives here and now, in you.
hope.practice: Remember the last time you got through something hard, and say out loud what your “invincible summer” was then.

quote.text: In the depths of winter, I finally learned that within me there lay an invincible summer.
quote.author: Albert Camus

nostalgia.text: Living in Paris, Camus returned in his thoughts to the Algerian sea all his life, and the very word “nostalgia” is a philosophical one for him. In The Myth of Sisyphus he speaks of the human “nostalgia” for unity, for clarity, for a world in which we would be “at home.” The absurd is precisely the meeting of this longing with the silence of the world. Camus does not call it a mistake: the longing for unity, in his words, expresses the essential impulse of the human drama. But his answer was not to live only in the past but to carry his love for it into the present. In this light, nostalgia is a sign of your deep attachment to the world, and you can accept it with tenderness.
nostalgia.practice: Find a small glimmer today of what you miss — a light, a smell, a tune — and linger on it for a minute.

craving.text: As a boy Camus spent hours on the beaches of Algiers, learning to stay afloat without fighting the waves. A sharp “I want it right now” is a lot like a wave, and there is nothing shameful in it. In The Myth of Sisyphus, Camus valued “lucidity” (lucidité) — the ability to see your situation honestly, without looking away. A craving promises a quick way out — out of tension, out of boredom, out of a question with no answer: “do this and it will get easier.” Camus did not condemn people for this thirst for relief: he understood too well how hard it is to live without guarantees. But he considered the living present, seen clearly, to be our greatest wealth. It means seeing the wave of desire as a wave — it rises, peaks and subsides — and remaining yourself, here, with your body, the light and the people around you.
craving.practice: Set a timer for five minutes and watch the craving like a wave from the shore: it rises, crests, falls. At the end, notice what it has become.

addiction.text: Camus liked to say that what he knew most surely about morality and duty he owed to football — to a team, where no one plays alone. Dependence is not a moral failure, and he never measured people by their purity. In The Myth of Sisyphus he spoke of the freedom of the absurd man: not a promise that everything will become easy, but the ability to see your life clearly and not hand it over entirely to any power — whether an idea, a fear or a habit. Getting out of a long-standing cycle resembles the way Camus understood revolt: not one great victory, but a daily, modest “no” to what narrows life and “yes” to what widens it. And Camus also insisted that revolt is never a solitary affair: it connects people who recognize a shared struggle in one another. There are always others nearby walking a similar path.
addiction.practice: If you feel like it, picture a mutual-help group as a team where no one plays alone, and say out loud one thing you would want them to understand about you.

hangover.text: Sun, water, air — Camus loved simple things, and on the morning after drinking, when the body aches, anxiety and shame rise and there are gaps in memory, they are the closest help. None of this makes you a bad person. Camus valued “lucidity” (lucidité) — the ability to look at things directly, without prettifying them and without blowing them up into a catastrophe. That means morning shame often offers two traps: pretending that nothing happened, or passing a final verdict on yourself. Camus trusted neither comforting illusions nor despair — both lead away from real life. Lucidity is simpler and gentler: admit that it was hard, calmly find out what you don’t remember if you need to, and return to those simple things. The body he wrote about with such tenderness needs care right now, not punishment.
hangover.practice: Step outside or go to a window for a minute and feel the air on your face. Tell yourself: “Today I look at this clearly — and without a verdict.”

euphoria.text: Sun, sea, the scent of herbs — and complete agreement with life: in Nuptials Camus describes moments when the boundary between a person and the world seems to disappear. He loved life with his whole body and would not have belittled such a burst. For him, such moments were not an illusion but a truth about how generous the world can be. But Camus also valued “lucidity”: joy does not need a promise that it will last forever, and it does not require the whole world to confirm that from now on everything will be different. Then euphoria can be lived fully — as a gift of this hour, without turning it into an oath to the future. Then even the comedown, if it comes, will not cancel what was.
euphoria.practice: Notice one sensation of this high — in your body, in the way you see, in sounds — and keep it as a gift of today, without promising yourself it will always be like this.

crash.text: Bread, conversation, a walk, the sun — Camus reminded us that almost all of real life lies between “all” and “nothing.” After a high, when yesterday the world was shining and today it is gray and cramped, that is easy to forget. This is not your fault. In The Rebel, Camus thought a great deal about the hunger for “all or nothing”: when a person wants the absolute, everything ordinary starts to look like nothing. Against this he set “measure” — not dull moderation, but the ability to love life as it is: neither shining forever nor empty. In other words, a comedown is often intensified by comparison: after the flash, an ordinary day looks gray, although it is simply ordinary. Camus did not reproach people for their longing for the absolute — he considered it deeply human. But he reminded us that an ordinary day is not “nothing.”
crash.practice: Name three ordinary things in today that are neither “everything” nor “nothing,” but are still here: a cup of tea, a phone call, the light in the window.

panic.text: From the age of seventeen Camus lived with tuberculosis and knew firsthand what it is to be suddenly afraid for your own breath. When your heart pounds and it seems that something irreversible is about to happen, it is genuinely frightening, and you are not exaggerating anything. His philosophy is largely about how to stay in the present when the mind is painting catastrophes. For Camus, what is most certain is not reasoning but what can be felt: in Nuptials the body itself knows the world — warm stone, sun, sea water. In this light, there is no need to argue with your thoughts during panic. You can return to what is certainly here: the ground under your feet, the objects around you, the air. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes.
panic.practice: Rest your palm on something solid and warm — a wall, a cup, your own knee — and say to yourself: “This is here.” Breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, and name five things you can see.

dread.text: Revolt, freedom, passion — three words Camus drew from the hardest question a person can ask: “what is it all for?” When the question of our own finitude rises, it is one of the hardest experiences there is, and Camus knew it from the inside. But his answer is unequivocal: life is worth living even if the world offers no ready-made meaning — and perhaps all the more fully for that. From awareness of the absurd, he drew exactly these three consequences. Revolt is the refusal to give up and the resolve to live with open eyes. Freedom is living without waiting for permission from above. Passion is the fullness of experiencing each day. Dread before the abyss is not the end of thought but its beginning: the moment when you see life at its full height. Camus believed that a person can stand before this and still love the sun, people and their day.
dread.practice: Write down one thing you love about today, however small: a taste, a voice, the light. Camus considered such things not trifles but the heart of life.

fomo.text: “What counts is not living best but living most,” Camus wrote in The Myth of Sisyphus — and at first glance the line only fuels the feeling that life is brighter somewhere else and you are late. But he meant not the number of places and events but the fullness of presence: feeling your own life as clearly and keenly as possible. Endless comparison with other people’s lives, by contrast, draws you out of your own day into an imaginary one. Camus loved the concrete: this beach, this morning, this conversation with a friend. For him, the grandeur of life was not somewhere else but here, under this sun. So the fear of missing out is not a verdict on your life but an invitation to return to it: the most important thing not to miss is happening where you are right now.
fomo.practice: Put your phone away and name out loud three details of your “here and now” that appear in no feed: a smell, a sound, the light in the room.

quote.text: Real generosity toward the future lies in giving all to the present.
quote.author: Albert Camus

sleepless.text: “Thought at the meridian” — that is Camus’s name for clarity on a human scale, and at three in the morning it is sorely missing. If you can’t sleep, there is nothing strange about everything seeming heavier at night. At the end of The Rebel, Camus speaks of “thought at the meridian” — clear, Mediterranean, on a human scale — as opposed to thought that runs off into extremes and absolutes. Night thoughts are often the opposite of noonday ones: in the dark, when nothing can be done, the mind inflates problems to cosmic proportions, and every question demands a final answer right now. Camus valued lucidity, but lucidity is not endless brooding; it is a calm gaze that comes most easily in daylight. That means you don’t have to believe your nighttime conclusions. They can be put off until morning, when the world is once again on your scale.
sleepless.practice: Tell the night thought: “I’ll come back to you in daylight.” Then shift your attention to the warmth of the blanket and a slow exhale.

betrayal.text: In The Rebel Camus writes that revolt begins with a simple feeling: there is a line that must not be crossed. When you have been betrayed, that line has been crossed, and your pain and anger are justified. Your inner “this is not okay” is not touchiness but the affirmation of a value: loyalty, honesty, respect. Camus held friendship and solidarity very high; in The Plague, Dr. Rieux and Tarrou hold on to each other in the midst of the epidemic, and this loyalty is one of the few things the calamity cannot take away. Then one person’s betrayal does not refute these values themselves. It hurts precisely because they are yours. And they are still alive — in other people and in you.
betrayal.practice: Get in touch with someone with whom loyalty is still alive for you — just to hear their voice.

jealousy.text: Camus hardly wrote about jealousy, but he had a precise name for its core — the “longing for clarity.” Jealousy is agonizing, and there is nothing shameful in it. We want to know for sure: what the other person feels, where they are, whether they will choose us tomorrow. And another person, like the world in Camus, gives no final guarantees. Camus called the absurd the collision of our hunger for clarity with the silence of the world; in jealousy this collision takes place inside love. Camus suggested neither pretending that there are guarantees nor giving up love. He valued love as a living presence here and now. In other words, you can acknowledge your anxiety without submitting to it entirely, and return to what is really there between you today.
jealousy.practice: Ask yourself: “What do I know for sure right now — and what am I filling in?” Write the answers as two short lists.

resentment.text: Revolt and hidden grievance grow from the same wound but go in opposite directions — one of the subtlest distinctions in The Rebel. Old resentment almost always has a real cause. Camus called the second ressentiment. Drawing on the philosopher Max Scheler, he described ressentiment as a self-poisoning: a feeling that stews for a long time in powerlessness, in a closed space, and turns against the person themselves. Revolt, by contrast, affirms: there is something valuable in me, and I am defending it. Camus did not demand that you forget or forgive. But he showed that from the same wound not only bitterness but also dignity can grow. In this light, your resentment can be recognized as legitimate — and gradually turned from poison into clear knowledge of your own worth and of what you will not allow again.
resentment.practice: Say out loud to yourself: “This resentment is protecting in me …” — and finish it. Perhaps there is a value behind it that is time to acknowledge.

heartbreak.text: When Oran was quarantined, lovers ended up on different sides of the city walls: in The Plague they go over memories, count the days and don’t know when the separation will end — Camus calls this “exile.” A broken heart aches just as sharply, and it shouldn’t be rushed. Camus writes about this pain with enormous compassion and without reproach. And he shows how people gradually learn to live inside it: not cancelling love, but finding ways to fill today — with work, friendship, care for others. From Camus’s point of view, love, even lost love, is not a mistake but one of the best things that can happen to a person. It was real, and how much it hurts speaks of its strength.
heartbreak.practice: Go for a short walk and notice three things along the way that fill the day with life rather than thoughts of the breakup.

impostor.text: Camus spent years staging plays and acting in them himself, and in The Myth of Sisyphus he devoted a whole chapter to the actor. If you are haunted by the sense of “I’m about to be found out,” that chapter is for you too. In a single evening the actor lives someone else’s life, knowing perfectly well that he is not Hamlet or a king — and yet he plays in earnest, giving himself wholly to the role. For Camus this is not deception but one of the images of human life itself: the world does not issue us a certificate proving we rightfully occupy our place. All of us, in some sense, play roles we have chosen or that have fallen to us. So impostor syndrome is not an exposure but a lucid view of a shared condition. And a role played in earnest is already work honestly done.
impostor.practice: Before your next task, imagine you are stepping onto a stage: straighten up, breathe in, and play your role in earnest. That is enough.

self_hatred.text: Clamence, the “judge-penitent,” accuses himself so that he can judge everyone else — Camus knew how the inner prosecutor works. When you hate yourself, its voice sounds like undeniable truth. But its verdict is not the truth about you. All his life Camus argued with systems that claim final knowledge about human beings and pass verdicts in their name. The inner critic works the same way: it gathers everything worst and passes it off as the complete portrait. Camus, however, saw in every person something that deserves respect — his whole idea of revolt rests on this. So you can rebel against the critic too: not arguing with its every word to the point of exhaustion, but saying “no” to its very role as judge. You are more than what it accuses you of — and you have every right to be on your own side.
self_hatred.practice: Say to the critic out loud, as a rebel would: “No — to your role as judge.” Then name one deed or quality you respect in yourself.

helplessness.text: The minor clerk Grand spends every evening after work carefully keeping statistics for the sanitary squads — and the narrator of The Plague suggests that he be considered the hero of the book. Helplessness is agonizing and often honestly reflects reality: some things do not depend on us. Camus did not deny this. In The Plague the townspeople cannot stop the epidemic, and no one knows when it will end. But the novel’s characters find what to do inside this helplessness. Then you need not demand of yourself that you change everything; you can look for your own small, concrete task. Camus believed that such modest participation is already a revolt against powerlessness, and that together people are capable of more than they are alone.
helplessness.practice: Name one very small thing that is within your power today, and do it as carefully as Grand kept his records.

procrastination.text: Grand in The Plague spends years rewriting the first sentence of his novel — about a horsewoman on a sorrel mare in the Bois de Boulogne — and cannot move on. If you are stuck at the start, it almost never comes down to laziness: often behind it is a fear that the result won’t live up to expectations, or a sense that the task is huge and pointless. Camus offers an unexpected perspective: the meaning of labor is not that the rock should stay at the top forever. Sisyphus knows the rock will roll down, and still he takes hold of it again. For Camus, what is valuable is the effort itself, the climb itself, not the final result. In other words, there is no need to wait for certainty that everything will turn out perfectly. You can simply put your hands on the rock — begin with the first small movement.
procrastination.practice: Do the first two minutes of the task — no more. Think not about the summit, only about the first push of the rock.

quote.text: The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart.
quote.author: Albert Camus

uprooted.text: Exile and the Kingdom — that is what Camus called his last collection of stories, and the title holds the whole story of moving away. Being cut off from home was something he knew personally. He was born and raised in Algeria and loved its sun and sea, but he had to live and work in France; longing for his native land runs through all his work. In that book (1957), losing one’s place and finding it are always close together. Camus did not suggest forgetting what was lost. He showed that a person can carry their native land within — in memory, in a love of light, in habits — and at the same time gradually find their “kingdom” where they are now: in work, in friendship, in a new landscape. In this light, your longing is faithfulness to what you love.
uprooted.practice: Recall one thing from home that you carry with you: a taste, a word, a habit. Find a way today to bring it briefly to life in your new place.

overload.text: Camus never knew social media, but he knew the bustle of Paris well, and all his life he set simple, dense things against it: sun on the skin, the sea, a conversation with a friend, honest work. When noise and the endless feed wear you out, weakness has nothing to do with it. In The Myth of Sisyphus he admitted that he cannot know the meaning of the world as a whole — but he can feel his own heart and touch the world close at hand. The feed promises knowledge of everything at once but gives not a single real touch. Camus valued “lucidity,” but lucidity is not a quantity of information; it is a quality of presence. Being tired of noise is how a living person responds when starved of the real. Sometimes the best answer is not to learn even more but to feel one single thing.
overload.practice: Put the screen aside for two minutes and choose one physical sensation — the taste of water, the wind, the warmth of your palms. Let that be enough for now.

unreality.text: “The stranger who at certain moments comes to meet us in a mirror” — this line from The Myth of Sisyphus describes the strange feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, is not quite real. It is hard to talk about, and it is often frightening. In The Myth of Sisyphus he writes about moments when the world suddenly becomes foreign and “dense”: a familiar landscape loses the meaning we had lent it, and the world slips away, becoming itself again. For Camus this is not madness but a moment of sudden clarity, when the usual veil falls away. But he did not leave a person in this estrangement: his answer is to return to the world through the body and the senses, through sun, water, touch, living conversation. So the world has not disappeared — it has only become unfamiliar for a while.
unreality.practice: Touch water — wash your hands or face — and describe the sensation to yourself: the temperature, the flow, the drops. Let the world answer your body.

awe.text: The ruins of Tipasa among flowers, the sea, the smell of wormwood, a sun in which a person seems to dissolve — Camus’s early essays, Nuptials (1938), are almost a hymn to wonder before the vast and beautiful. It was one of the experiences he held most dear. Camus called this a “nuptial” with the world — a union in which nothing needs to be explained or earned. There he also writes that he understands what glory is: the right to love without measure. For him, awe does not contradict the clear knowledge that life is finite and the world gives no guarantees. On the contrary, it was precisely knowing this that made him cherish such moments so keenly. That means awe is not an escape from reality but the fullest encounter with it. You can simply live it through to the end.
awe.practice: Stay for a minute with whatever filled you with awe, breathing slowly and adding nothing. Then tell yourself: “I saw this.”

relief.text: The gates of Oran open, people dance in the streets, those who were separated find each other again — the ending of The Plague is one of the best-known images of relief in literature. This feeling is worth living to the full, without hurrying on. Camus describes this joy with enormous tenderness and makes no attempt to mute it. Dr. Rieux, the narrator, decides to write down what was lived through, to bear witness for those who suffered and to the fact that there is more in people to admire than to despise. Relief in Camus is not forgetting but grateful lucidity: the hard time was real, and the fact that it has passed is real too. Allow yourself both.
relief.practice: Take a few slow breaths out, like someone walking through open gates, and say out loud what helped you hold on.

calm.text: After the hard years of the war, Camus came back to the ruins of Tipasa by the sea and found there the silence and light that had seemed lost — this is the essay “Return to Tipasa.” Peace and quiet are precious, and he knew their worth. For Camus, calm is not an escape from the world or indifference, but moments of agreement with it, when there is nothing to achieve or prove. Such moments, for Camus, give a person back the strength to live, work and care for others again. Calm is not a luxury or idleness but part of the same faithfulness to life as revolt. It needs no justification. You can simply be in it, like being by the sea on a clear day.
calm.practice: Sit for a couple of minutes listening to the quietest sound around you. Don’t try to achieve anything — just be where you are.

inspiration.text: Camus called the creator “the most absurd of men” — in the best sense: he creates with no guarantee that what he makes will be eternal or understood, and still gives himself wholly to the work. Inspiration is a joyful, living state, and Camus knew it as a writer and a man of the theater. To create, for Camus, is to live doubly: to see the world anew and more vividly and to give it form. He believed art should not run away from reality — it brings us back to it, to people, to light, to our shared fate. In this light, inspiration is not a whim but a special fullness of presence. There is no need to hold on to it by force: you can simply follow it today.
inspiration.practice: Write down one phrase, image or melody that has come to you now. Don’t judge it — just give it a place on paper.

schadenfreude.text: In an Amsterdam bar, Clamence talks with merciless irony about his own vanity — Camus presented such confessions without disdain. Almost everyone knows schadenfreude, though few admit to it. Camus valued “lucidity” (lucidité) — an honest, unembellished look at oneself — so simply admitting such a feeling is already in his spirit. Clamence also dissects his secret pleasure in feeling superior to others; Camus shows that such impulses exist in many people who consider themselves perfectly decent. Camus would probably say that schadenfreude is often born of a sense that you alone are pushing your rock uphill, and someone else’s failure proves for a moment that others have it hard too. But behind this lies an important truth: we are all in the same boat. The absurd is shared, and another person’s failure can become not a reason to feel superior but a reminder of solidarity.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: “Where in my life right now is the rock that made me want someone else to struggle too?” Write down the answer.

contempt.text: At the end of The Plague, Dr. Rieux, who has seen both cowardice and baseness, concludes that there are more things to admire in people than to despise. When someone seems petty, dishonest or cruel to you, that feeling doesn’t come from nowhere. Camus knew this feeling and was attentive to it. In The Rebel he wrote that genuine revolt defends human dignity — including the dignity of the person it is directed against; a revolt that begins to despise people loses its “measure” and betrays itself. Camus would probably say that contempt is a “no” said to a whole person, whereas it is more honest to say “no” to a specific act. You can see another’s weakness clearly and still not deny them the fate you share.
contempt.practice: Say two sentences out loud to yourself: “In this act I do not accept …” and “And still we share a fate in that …”

quote.text: …there are more things to admire in men than to despise.
quote.author: Albert Camus

disgust.text: A man is talking on the phone behind a glass partition: you can’t hear the words, only see his silent gestures, and they suddenly seem senseless — with this scene from The Myth of Sisyphus Camus describes a sudden estrangement. Disgust — with people, a situation, sometimes yourself — can be just as sudden and strong. Suddenly the familiar world becomes foreign, people seem mechanical, their gestures devoid of meaning. Importantly, Camus did not stop at disgust. He saw it as a moment of awakening: mechanical life has cracked, and you have seen it from the outside. After that a choice is possible — not to turn away from the world but to return to it with clear eyes. So Dr. Rieux in The Plague sees in people both filth and weakness, and still keeps coming to them. Disgust is neither a verdict on the world nor a verdict on you.
disgust.practice: Turn your eyes away from what disgusts you and find one small thing nearby that is pleasant to look at: light, a leaf, a cup. Stay with it for a minute.

revenge.text: All his life Camus argued against “an eye for an eye,” yet he never pretended the urge to strike back was foreign to him. When you have been wronged, you want to restore the upset balance. In “Reflections on the Guillotine” he wrote that the ancient law of retaliation, “an eye for an eye,” is rooted in nature and instinct, not in law — that is, it is a natural impulse but a poor basis for action. In The Rebel he showed how revolt against injustice, once it forgets “measure,” begins to commit new injustice of its own. From Camus’s point of view, behind revenge there is usually a right “no”: you cannot treat me like this. That “no” is worth keeping and respecting. But it can be expressed differently — by defending your boundary, naming what happened out loud, refusing to put up with it any longer — without becoming the one who hurt you.
revenge.practice: Complete: “I was hurt, and my ‘no’ means that …” Then: “I can defend this boundary without causing harm, like this: …”

anger_at_loved.text: A “no” that at the same time says “yes” — this is Camus’s formula for revolt, and with loved ones it is especially clear. Being furious with a partner, parents or children is very human, and the shame after an outburst shows how much they matter to you. Anger usually says “no” not to the whole person but to what has become unbearable: exhaustion, misunderstanding, a recurring hurt. And the “yes” in it is to the relationship itself, in which you want to be heard. Camus insisted on “measure”: genuine revolt does not destroy what it arose for. In other words, you need not be ashamed of the anger itself; you can ask what “yes” stands behind it — and take care that its form does not wound those you love. Anger expressed in words rather than blows is also revolt, only with measure.
anger_at_loved.practice: Before you answer someone close, take three slow breaths out and ask yourself: “What ‘yes’ stands behind my ‘no’?” Then say it in words, not in tone.

ambivalence.text: “Between Yes and No” is what Camus called one of his first essays, from the book Betwixt and Between. There he writes about his mother — silent, almost deaf, distant — and infinitely dear; to cherish someone close and at the same time be unable to stand them is not a flaw of character but the ordinary truth of closeness. His love for her was woven of tenderness and estrangement at once, and he did not try to choose one. Camus was generally wary of attempts to reduce life to a single clear formula. He proposed “lucidity” — keeping both sides in view, the wrong side and the right side. In this light, mixed feelings are not an error to be urgently corrected. They are honest knowledge about a person who matters to you so much that they stir everything at once.
ambivalence.practice: Divide a page in half: “the wrong side” and “the right side.” In each half write one feeling toward this person, without crossing any out.

guilty_relief.text: The city rejoices, people embrace in the streets — and in the same crowd walk those who have lost someone: this is how Camus ends The Plague. Relief you feel ashamed of — after a breakup, a departure, after the death of a loved one who was ill for a long time — is a very common and almost always hidden feeling. The narrator condemns neither the joy nor the grief: they simply exist side by side. For Camus, honesty about your own feelings matters more than matching what you are “supposed” to feel; The Stranger is in many ways a novel about how society demands the correct emotions. Relief does not cancel love. It speaks of how long you carried the weight, and of the fact that life goes on in you. Love and relief can both be true at once.
guilty_relief.practice: Write one sentence that holds both feelings: “I feel lighter, and I still love …” Read it to yourself without justifying anything.

indifference.text: “Mother died today. Or maybe yesterday, I don’t know” — so begins The Stranger, Camus’s most famous novel about silence where something “should” move you. If it is quiet inside you too, and the quiet is joined by the worry “what is wrong with me?”, you are not alone. Meursault does not cry at his mother’s funeral, and the court judges him partly for that. In the preface to the American edition, Camus wrote that Meursault is condemned because he does not play the game: he refuses to lie, that is, to say more than he feels. Camus would probably say that indifference does not always mean heartlessness. Sometimes feelings come later; sometimes numbness protects us from something too strong. Honestly admitting “right now I don’t feel what is expected of me” is already a form of “lucidity.” Your inner state does not have to match other people’s expectations.
indifference.practice: Sit for a minute and honestly note what you actually feel — even if it is “almost nothing.” Tell yourself: “I don’t have to say more than I feel.”

escape.text: The journalist Rambert, trapped in plague-stricken Oran, tries with all his might to reach the woman he loves — and Dr. Rieux does not condemn him. The urge to drop everything was something Camus understood from within. Camus described how it arises in The Myth of Sisyphus: rising, streetcar, work, lunch, work again, sleep — day after day, until one day the question “why?” arises. He called this the moment when “the stage sets collapse” and considered it not a breakdown but an awakening. Rieux does not condemn Rambert: Camus considered the wish for happiness legitimate. What to choose — to stay or to leave — is for each person to decide, and Camus gave no ready-made recipes. That means the wish to escape is a signal that you have once again asked about the meaning of your everyday life. It is a valuable question, and it does not need an immediate answer.
escape.practice: Walk for five minutes with no destination and ask yourself as you go: “What do I want to leave — and what do I want to reach?” Don’t decide anything.

forbidden_attraction.text: The Myth of Sisyphus has a chapter on Don Juan, and Camus writes about him without moralizing. Attraction to someone who is unavailable or “wrong” can be very strong and confusing. Camus saw the human being above all as a hunger — for clarity, unity, fullness of life. He called it a “nostalgia” for unity and considered it an inseparable part of us. The absurd, for Camus, arises where this hunger meets a world that does not answer it the way we want. Forbidden attraction is a very vivid case of such a collision: the desire is strong, and circumstances say “no.” Camus warned against two escapes: the “leap” into self-condemnation and the illusion that a single desire can answer everything. Camus would probably say that seeing your desire clearly means neither obeying it nor being ashamed of it. You can simply ask honestly what fullness of life it is speaking of.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Ask yourself not about them but about yourself: “Around them I feel …” — and think about where else in your life that quality could be found.

social_anxiety.text: “Don’t wait for the Last Judgment. It takes place every day,” says Clamence in The Fall — and anyone shy of other people’s eyes knows that thought well. Camus understood the power of other people’s judgment well. But Camus shows Clamence as a man caught in a trap: he is so afraid of judgment that he himself becomes a perpetual judge. Camus himself sought the opposite — living camaraderie. He loved the theater precisely for the teamwork, where people do something together instead of evaluating one another. Camus would probably note that most of the people around you are also afraid of others’ eyes; this fear is part of our shared human fate. If for a moment you see the people you are talking to not as judges but as equally uncertain human beings, the fear won’t disappear, but it will become a little lighter.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, imagine that you and the other person are on one team, as on a football pitch, not judge and defendant. Notice what changes in your body.

uncertainty.text: “Living without appeal” — that is what Camus called a life that doesn’t wait for everything to become clear. When you don’t know what will happen and there is nothing to lean on, it is hard. For Camus this is not an accidental misfortune but the basic condition of life. The world gives no guarantees and does not answer our question “how will it all end?” That means not postponing life until the day when everything finally becomes clear, because that day may never come. But his conclusion is life-affirming: if the future is not guaranteed, the present becomes all the more precious. You can not know what will happen and still live fully today — work, love, notice the sun. The uncertainty remains, but it stops being the only thing you see.
uncertainty.practice: Write: “I don’t know how this will end. But today I can …” — and finish with one small thing that depends on you.

waiting.text: Sealed-off Oran in The Plague lives in constant expectation — of letters that don’t arrive, of news, of the end of the epidemic — and Camus calls this feeling “exile”: people are home, it seems, yet their thoughts are always somewhere in the future. Waiting for results, an answer, news can feel agonizingly long. Some count the days from morning to night; others — like the modest clerk Grand, stubbornly rewriting a single sentence of his book, or the doctors and volunteers — keep doing their work. Camus does not reproach those who wait; he simply shows that waiting is easier when there is something to do in it, here and now. Camus would probably say that waiting need not be drowned out, but you don’t have to give it your whole day either. The present hasn’t gone anywhere while you wait.
waiting.practice: For the next hour, choose one small task unrelated to what you are waiting for, and do it completely.

regret.text: Clamence in The Fall carries for years a single moment when he failed to help someone in danger — this is how Camus explored regret. If the past keeps coming back to you, the book has a great deal to say. But Camus shows what regret turns into when it is not lived through: Clamence endlessly passes sentence on himself, and on everyone else along the way — he becomes a “judge-penitent.” The book is a warning: perpetual judgment of yourself does not make you better and helps no one. Camus himself valued something else — “lucidity” and action. The past cannot be changed, but you can honestly name what happened and ask what you can do now, in the life you have. Then regret is not a verdict but knowledge of what matters to you.
regret.practice: Say out loud in one sentence what you regret, and then take one small action in the spirit of the value this regret reveals.

longing.text: Throughout the epidemic Dr. Rieux lives apart from his wife, who has gone to the mountains for treatment, and waits for her letters. Longing for a particular person is one of the sharpest forms of love. Camus described it in The Plague: when the city was sealed off, many were cut off from those they loved. He writes that the first thing the plague brought was “exile,” and that those separated lived on memories and imagined conversations, counted the days, reread old letters. Camus does not condemn longing or call on us to drown it out; for him it is an honest side of love, which does not cease to exist across distance. But he also shows that people, while longing, went on living and helping one another. That means longing is not emptiness but the presence of love. You can carry it without giving up your day.
longing.practice: Write this person a short thought or letter, even if you never send it. Then do one thing they would be glad to see in your day.

world_pain.text: “I rebel — therefore we exist”: Camus’s formula grew out of the experience of war and occupation. Pain for the world — from grim news, wars, injustice — can be almost unbearable. Camus wrote The Plague as a book about a calamity that falls on everyone and about how people endure it. His heroes are not superheroes. Dr. Rieux, asked what gives him strength, answers simply: not heroism but decency, that is, doing his job. Tarrou explains that in any calamity he wants to be on the side of the victims. Camus does not demand that you save the whole world. He offers what is within everyone’s reach: not looking away, not lying to yourself, and doing the little you can, together with others. That formula says that even sharp pain for the world unites us with people rather than separating us from them.
world_pain.practice: Choose one small, real action for this week — to help, support, call someone. And for today, the news can wait an hour.

quote.text: The only means of fighting a plague is common decency.
quote.author: Albert Camus

rejection.text: Paris in the early fifties: Camus’s book is savaged in the journals, yesterday’s friends, Sartre among them, turn away from him, and for years he feels like an outsider. Rejection hurts, especially when you have opened up and heard “no.” He did not stop writing. Camus would probably say that rejection is one more encounter with a world that does not answer our call the way we would like. He did not promise that an answer would come. But he showed that the value of your “rock” — your work, your love, your way of living — is not determined by whether you were accepted or not. Sisyphus, rejected by the gods, goes on his way, and Camus invites us to imagine him happy.
rejection.practice: Spend five minutes today on your own work — the thing that stays yours regardless of anyone’s “yes” or “no” — like Camus, who did not stop writing.

abandonment.text: Camus’s father was killed in the First World War before his son was a year old, and his mother was silent and distant — he wrote about this early loss in The First Man, his last, unfinished book. The fear of being left runs deep, sometimes all the way back to childhood. His philosophy contains a similar motif: the absurd is felt as “the silence of the world” — as if the universe does not answer. But from this feeling Camus drew not despair but solidarity: since the world is silent, people need one another all the more. His characters find support not in guarantees but in friendship, shared work, simple human tenderness. In this light, your fear speaks of a deep need for connection. It cannot be insured, but it can be cultivated — including with the people who are already near you.
abandonment.practice: Send one person you feel at ease with a few simple words today — for no particular reason.

unrequited.text: A person calls out, and the world stays silent — this is how Camus defined the absurd, and unrequited love is the absurd in miniature. You turn to someone with your whole heart, the answer is silence or a polite “no,” and it wounds deeply. Camus advised neither pretending that an answer will come nor devaluing your call. He proposed a third way — “lucidity”: seeing that there is no answer and still not renouncing what was alive in you. The capacity to love so strongly is, for Camus, one of the things that make up the very fullness of life. Your love was not a mistake because it went unanswered. It testifies that you know how to love. That capacity stays with you — and one day it will again find somewhere to go.
unrequited.practice: Write down three things this love revealed in you: what you learned about yourself, about your tenderness, about what matters to you.

humiliation.text: As a boy Camus lived in a cramped flat in a working-class neighborhood of Algiers and learned early what it is to be on the lowest rung. Humiliation wounds deeply: it feels as though your dignity has been taken away. In The Myth of Sisyphus he retells the myth of a man the gods punished with futile labor: forever rolling a rock up a mountain, only for it to roll back down. And yet Camus writes that at the moment when Sisyphus walks back down toward his rock and becomes conscious of his fate, he is superior to his fate — he is stronger than his rock. So dignity cannot be taken from outside: it lies in a clear view of what is happening and in refusing to accept that someone else’s disdain determines your worth. Humiliation speaks of the other person’s act, not of who you are.
humiliation.practice: Stand up, straighten your shoulders and breathe out slowly, like Sisyphus on the way down, looking clearly at his rock. Tell yourself: “My dignity is still mine.”

body_shame.text: The beaches of Algiers, sun on the skin, swimming in the sea — in the essay “Summer in Algiers” Camus writes that there the body lives and rejoices openly. Dissatisfaction with your body can be a constant background of life, and this view can shift it a little. For Camus, the body is not a picture to be rated but a way of being in the world: through it we feel water, warmth, wind, the tiredness after work. That means dissatisfaction with ourselves often arises when we look at the body only from the outside, as an image. Camus offers a view from within: the body is your way to the sun, the sea, embraces and movement. It does not have to be perfect to give you this encounter with the world.
body_shame.practice: For a minute, pay attention not to how your body looks but to what it feels: warmth, support, breath. Name one pleasant sensation.

illness.text: At seventeen Camus, a football goalkeeper, learned that he had tuberculosis — he had to give up football, and later the illness closed off a teaching career to him. When the body lets you down, it takes away strength, plans and your familiar sense of yourself. And yet it was after this that he wrote his sunniest essays — about the sea, light and love of the world. For Camus, lucidity meant not closing your eyes to the body’s fragility and, at the same time, not handing your whole life over to the illness. For Camus, even within limitations there remains room for what he valued most: friendship, thought, beauty, small joys. Illness changes your path, but it does not cancel your presence in the world.
illness.practice: Notice one small thing that brings joy or calm today despite how you feel: light, a sound, a taste, the voice of someone dear.

pride.text: “The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man’s heart,” Camus writes in the last lines of The Myth of Sisyphus. Pride in what you have done is a healthy and well-earned feeling; there is no need to hide it. In The Plague, the narrator suggests that the true hero is not some brilliant figure but the modest clerk Grand — for the bit of goodness in his heart and his persistence in his work. Camus valued pride not in superiority over others but in honestly accomplished work. His Sisyphus is happy not because the rock has finally stayed at the top but because the struggle toward the summit is his own. In other words, your pride is the recognition that you have put yourself into something real. You can enjoy it — calmly, without apologies and without comparing yourself to others.
pride.practice: Tell someone in one sentence what you are proud of and the effort behind it — without apologies and without comparisons.

melancholy.text: Roman ruins by the sea, flooded with sunlight, the smell of herbs — in his essay on Tipasa Camus describes a joy in which one can hear the thought that everything passes. Bright sadness, where sorrow and tenderness toward the world are intertwined, was well known to him. For Camus, love of the world and a clear understanding of its fragility do not contradict each other — on the contrary, they strengthen each other. Melancholy, then, is neither an illness nor a defeat but a special sensitivity: you see beauty and at the same time know it is fleeting. Camus did not urge us to get rid of this note; he urged us not to turn away from the light in which it sounds. Bright sadness can simply be lived — like a warm evening you don’t try to stop.
melancholy.practice: Find something beautiful and fleeting nearby — light, a cloud, a sound. Look at it for a minute, doing nothing with whatever feeling comes.
